This is Yahweh’s verdict on Jehoiakim king of Judah: Nobody from his family will sit on David’s throne. His corpse will lie outside, in daytime heat and nighttime frost.
For their guilt I will punish him, his children, and his servants. On them, on the people of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah I will bring every disaster I announced. They would not listen.’”

Jeremiah took another scroll and handed it to Baruch, who was Neriah’s son and a secretary. Jeremiah spoke, and Baruch wrote every word of the book that King Jehoiakim of Judah had burned. Many more words like them were added.

notes.text: That is, 605-604 B.C., the year of the battle of Carchemish (46:2).
Hebrew “a scroll of a book,” a roll made of papyrus or leather.
Hebrew “from the mouth of Jeremiah.” The same idea is used for “as I spoke” in verses 6, 17, 27, and 32.
Hebrew atsur, “held back” or “blocked.” The reason is not given. The Septuagint reads “I am in trouble.”
That is, 604-603 B.C. The Septuagint reads “in the eighth year.”
Hebrew “the ninth month,” Kislev. A fast may have been called because of the Babylonian army’s advance.
Hebrew “the ninth month,” Kislev, the cold, rainy season.
Hebrew delatot, “doors,” that is, columns of writing on the scroll.
The Septuagint reverses the sense: “But Elnathan and Gedaliah urged the king to burn the scroll.”

verses.text: Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon made Zedekiah son of Josiah king of Judah, to rule in the place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim.
Yet Zedekiah, along with his servants and the common people, disregarded the words Yahweh spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.

King Zedekiah sent a message to the prophet Jeremiah by two men. One was Jehucal,{a} whose father was Shelemiah. The other was Zephaniah the priest, whose father was Maaseiah. They said, “Please pray to Yahweh our God for us.”
Jeremiah could still walk around among the people at that point. Nobody had locked him up yet.
Meanwhile, Pharaoh’s army had left Egypt. The Chaldeans who had Jerusalem surrounded heard about it and backed away from the city.{b}
Then Yahweh gave Jeremiah the prophet a message.
“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this. The king of Judah sent you to learn My will. Tell him: Pharaoh’s army marched out to help you, but it will return to its own land, Egypt.
The Chaldeans will come again. They will attack this city, take it, and set it on fire.
Yahweh says: Do not fool yourselves by thinking, ‘The Chaldeans will surely leave us alone.’ They will not leave.
Even if you beat the whole Chaldean army that is fighting you, and only injured men were left lying in their tents, those men would still rise up and set this city ablaze.”
The Chaldean army had pulled away from Jerusalem because Pharaoh’s army was coming.
At that time Jeremiah left Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin and claim his share{c} among his relatives.
He reached the Benjamin Gate. A guard captain was posted there, named Irijah, son of Shelemiah and grandson of Hananiah. He grabbed Jeremiah and shouted, “You are deserting to the Chaldeans!”
“That is a lie!” Jeremiah said. “I am not deserting to the Chaldeans.” But Irijah would not listen. He arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials.
The officials were furious with Jeremiah. They beat him and threw him in jail. They had turned the house of Jonathan the secretary into a prison.
So Jeremiah was put in the dungeon,{d} in one of its vaulted cells, and he stayed there many days.
After a while King Zedekiah had him fetched and questioned him privately in the palace. “Has Yahweh given you a message?” Jeremiah answered, “Yes. The king of Babylon will receive you from them.”
Then Jeremiah asked King Zedekiah, “What wrong did I do to you, to your servants, or to this people? Why have you thrown me in prison?
Where are your prophets now? They told you, ‘Babylon’s king will never come against you or this land.’
Now please listen, my lord the king. Hear my request. Do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary. I would die there.”

King Zedekiah gave the order, and Jeremiah was moved to the guard’s yard. A round loaf of bread was brought to him each day from the Street of the Bakers, until the city ran out of bread. And so Jeremiah stayed in the guard’s yard.

notes.text: Jehucal means “Yahweh is able.” He is called Jucal in 38:1. A clay seal with the name “Yehukal son of Shelemiah” has been found in Jerusalem.
This lifting of the siege is the setting for 34:21-22 too.
The meaning of the Hebrew is not certain. It may mean receiving a share of a family inheritance (compare Jeremiah 32:8).
Hebrew “the house of the cistern,” a dungeon under the ground.

verses.text: Four men heard what Jeremiah was telling everyone: Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur son of Malchiah.
He had said, “Yahweh says: Those who stay in this city will die by sword, hunger, or sickness. Those who walk out to the Chaldeans will survive. Their lives will be their prize of war.{a}
Yahweh says: This city will definitely be handed to the army of Babylon’s king, and he will take it.”

The officials told the king, “This man must be put to death. His words are weakening the soldiers still in the city, and everyone else too. He does not want good for these people. He wants them ruined.”
King Zedekiah answered, “Do what you want with him. The king has no power to stop you.”

So they seized Jeremiah and dropped him into the well of Malchiah, the king’s son, which was in the guard’s yard. They let him down on ropes. The well held mud but no water, and Jeremiah sank into the mud.
Ebed-Melech,{b} a man from Cush who served as an officer in the palace, heard that Jeremiah had been put in the well. The king was sitting at the Benjamin Gate at the time.
Ebed-Melech hurried out of the palace and said to the king,
“My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in everything they did to Jeremiah the prophet. They threw him into a well, where he will starve, because the city has no bread left.”
Then the king gave Ebed-Melech the Cushite an order. “Take thirty men{c} with you. Lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the well before death takes him.”
Ebed-Melech took the men with him into the palace, to a spot beneath the storeroom. He collected some old rags and worn-out clothes there, and lowered them by rope down to Jeremiah.
Ebed-Melech the Cushite told Jeremiah, “Put these rags and old clothes under your arms, over the ropes.” Jeremiah did it.
Then the men hauled Jeremiah up with the ropes and got him out of the well. Jeremiah stayed in the guard’s yard.
King Zedekiah sent a messenger for Jeremiah the prophet. He met him at the third entrance to Yahweh’s house. “I want to ask you something,” the king said. “Hide nothing from me.”
Jeremiah replied, “If I answer, you will surely put me to death. If I advise you, you will not listen.”
Quietly, King Zedekiah vowed to Jeremiah, “As surely as Yahweh lives, the One who gave us breath, I will not put you to death. I will not give you to those men who are trying to kill you.”

Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “This is the word of Yahweh, the God of Armies, the God of Israel: If you surrender to the officers of Babylon’s king, you will keep your life. This city will not go up in flames. You and your household will survive.
But if you do not surrender to the officers of Babylon’s king, the Chaldeans will receive this city. They will set it on fire, and you will not slip away from them.”
King Zedekiah answered Jeremiah, “I fear the Judeans who have switched sides to the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans might turn me over to them, and they would treat me cruelly.”
Jeremiah said, “That will not happen. Please obey Yahweh by doing what I tell you. Then you will do well, and you will stay alive.
Yahweh has shown me what will happen if you will not go out.

Think of it: every woman still left in the palace of Judah’s king will be marched out to the officers of Babylon’s king. And they will say,
‘The friends you trusted{d} fooled you.
They overpowered you.
Your feet have sunk into the mud,
and they have deserted you.’
All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans. You will not escape either. Babylon’s king will seize you, and this city will burn{e} to the ground.”
Zedekiah then told Jeremiah, “Let nobody learn about this conversation, and you will live.
The officials may hear that I spoke with you. They may come and ask, ‘What did you say to the king? What did the king say to you? Tell us, and do not hide it, and we will not kill you.’
If so, then answer them, ‘My request to the king was that he not return me to Jonathan’s house, where I would die.’”
Every one of the officials came to Jeremiah and questioned him. He gave them the answer the king had ordered. So they stopped, because no one had overheard the conversation.
Jeremiah remained in the guard’s yard until Jerusalem fell.{f}

notes.text: Hebrew “his life will be his as loot,” that is, he will escape with his life and nothing more.
Ebed-Melech means “servant of the king.” He was a Cushite, from the upper Nile region (Nubia). Cush is sometimes called Ethiopia.
So the Hebrew and the Septuagint. One Hebrew copy is said to read “three men.”
Hebrew “the men of your peace.” These lines echo Obadiah 7.
So the ancient versions. The Hebrew reads “and you will burn this city,” that is, you will be the cause.
The last part of the Hebrew, “and it came to pass when Jerusalem was taken,” begins 39:1.

verses.text: In the tenth month (in December–January){a} of Zedekiah’s ninth year as king of Judah, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They surrounded the city.
In the fourth month (in June–July){b} of Zedekiah’s eleventh year, on the ninth day, the enemy broke through the city wall.

Every officer of Babylon’s king entered and took a seat in the Middle Gate. They were Nergal-Sharezer, Samgar-Nebo, Sarsechim the Rab-Saris, Nergal-Sharezer the Rab-Mag,{c} and the rest of Babylon’s officers.

King Zedekiah of Judah saw them,{d} and so did all his soldiers. They ran. They left the city at night by the king’s garden, going through the gate between the two walls. They headed toward the Arabah.

But the Chaldean army chased them. They caught Zedekiah in the plains near Jericho. They arrested him and took him to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath. There Nebuchadrezzar announced his sentence.
There at Riblah, Babylon’s king had Zedekiah’s sons put to death in front of their father. He also had all the nobles of Judah killed.
Then he blinded Zedekiah and chained him with bronze chains to take him to Babylon.
The Chaldeans burned down the king’s palace and the people’s homes. They tore down the walls of Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan,{e} the commander of the guard, took away the people who were left in the city. He took those who had gone over to his side, and everyone else who remained, as prisoners to Babylon.
But Nebuzaradan, the guard commander, allowed a few of the poorest people, who owned nothing, to stay in Judah. He gave them vineyards and fields on that very day.
Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon gave an order about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the guard commander.
“Find him and take good care of him. Do not let any harm come to him. Give him whatever he requests.”
So Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-Saris, Nergal-Sharezer the Rab-Mag, and all the other chief officers of Babylon’s king sent men.
They brought Jeremiah out of the guard’s yard and placed him under the protection of Gedaliah,{f} Ahikam’s son and a grandson of Shaphan. Gedaliah took him home. So Jeremiah lived among the people.
While Jeremiah was locked in the guard’s yard, Yahweh had given him a message.

“Go and tell Ebed-Melech the Cushite: ‘Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Watch! I will make My words about this city come true. They will bring disaster, not good, and you will see it happen on that day.
I will deliver you when that day comes,” Yahweh announces. “You will not fall into the hands of the men you fear.
I will surely rescue you. You will not die by the sword. You will escape with your life as a prize, because you trusted Me,” Yahweh announces.’”

notes.text: Hebrew “the tenth month,” Tevet. That is January 588 B.C. (compare 52:4; 2 Kings 25:1). The Septuagint does not have verses 4-13.
Hebrew “the fourth month,” Tammuz. That is July 587 or 586 B.C. Scholars disagree on the exact year.
Rab-saris and Rab-mag are Babylonian titles, perhaps “chief official” and “chief magician.” Nergal-Sharezer means “Nergal, protect the king.”
Verses 4-13 are not in the Septuagint. Verses 4-10 are very close to 52:7-16 and 2 Kings 25:4-12.
Nebuzaradan comes from the Babylonian Nabu-zer-iddin, “Nabu has given a child.” His title, rab-tabbachim, means “chief of the guard” or “chief cook.”
Gedaliah means “Yahweh is great.” He was the son of Ahikam, who had protected Jeremiah (26:24). The king of Babylon made him governor.

verses.text: Yahweh gave Jeremiah a message after Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, released him at Ramah. Nebuzaradan had found Jeremiah in chains among the captives from Jerusalem and Judah, who were on their way to exile in Babylon.{a}
The commander of the guard called Jeremiah over. He said, “Yahweh your God announced this disaster against this place.
Now Yahweh has made it happen, just as He said. It came because you people sinned against Yahweh and would not obey Him. So this has fallen on you.

Look, today I am freeing your hands from these chains. If you would like to travel with me to Babylon, come along, and I will take care of you. If not, stay. You may go anywhere in this land. Choose whatever place seems best to you.

Jeremiah still hesitated.{b} So Nebuzaradan added, “Then return to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, Shaphan’s grandson. Babylon’s king has made him ruler over Judah’s towns. You can stay with him among your people, or you can choose any other place.” The commander gave him food and a gift and sent him on his way.
Jeremiah went to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah.{c} He lived there with him among the people still left in the land.

Army officers and their men were still out in the countryside. News reached them that Babylon’s king had made Gedaliah son of Ahikam governor of the land. They heard he was responsible for the men, women, and children, the poorest people in the land, who had not been carried off to Babylon.

They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. The leaders were Ishmael{d} son of Nethaniah; Kareah’s sons Johanan{e} and Jonathan; Seraiah son of Tanhumeth; Ephai’s sons, from Netophah; and Jezaniah, whose father was a Maacathite. Each man brought his soldiers.
Gedaliah son of Ahikam, Shaphan’s grandson, gave his word to them and to their men. “Have no fear of serving the Chaldeans. Settle in this land and be loyal to Babylon’s king. You will do well.
I myself will stay at Mizpah to speak for you when the Chaldeans visit us. You should gather the wine, the summer fruit, and the olive oil. Store them in jars and settle in the towns you have taken.”

Judeans in Moab, Ammon, Edom, and other lands heard the news too. They heard that the king of Babylon had left some people in Judah and had made Gedaliah son of Ahikam, Shaphan’s grandson, governor over them.
So they all returned from the countries where they had been scattered. They arrived in Judah, at Mizpah, to see Gedaliah. They brought in a very large crop of wine and summer fruit.
Then Johanan son of Kareah came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, together with all the army leaders who had been in the countryside.
They told him, “Are you aware that Baalis{f} king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to murder you?” But Gedaliah son of Ahikam did not believe them.

Then Johanan son of Kareah talked to Gedaliah alone at Mizpah. “Let me go and kill Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Nobody will find out. Why let him murder you? Then all the Judeans around you would be scattered, and Judah’s last survivors would be lost.”
But Gedaliah son of Ahikam said to Johanan son of Kareah, “Do not do it. You are lying about Ishmael.”

notes.text: The words “A message came to Jeremiah” are not followed by a prophecy until 42:7.
The Hebrew is hard. Perhaps “before he could answer.”
Mizpah means “watchtower.” It was a town in Benjamin, often thought to be Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem.
Ishmael means “God hears.” He came from the royal family (41:1).
Johanan means “Yahweh has been kind.”
Baalis may mean “son of delight.” A seal found by diggers may name “Baalyisha king of the Ammonites.”

verses.text: It was the seventh month (in September–October).{a} Ishmael arrived at Mizpah to see Gedaliah son of Ahikam. His father was Nethaniah and his grandfather was Elishama. Ishmael belonged to the royal line and had served as a top officer of the king. Ten men came with him. As they all ate together at Mizpah,
Ishmael and his ten men sprang up. With their swords they cut down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, Shaphan’s grandson. So Ishmael murdered the man Babylon’s king had placed over the land.
Ishmael killed every Judean who was with Gedaliah in Mizpah as well. He also killed the Chaldean soldiers stationed there.
On the second day after the murder of Gedaliah, when nobody outside knew yet,

Eighty men came in from Shechem, Shiloh,{b} and Samaria, their beards shaved off and their clothes ripped. They had gashed themselves in mourning. In their hands were grain gifts and incense for Yahweh’s house.{c}
Ishmael son of Nethaniah left Mizpah to greet them, sobbing as he walked. As soon as he reached them he told them, “Please come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.”
Once they were in the middle of the town, Ishmael and his men slaughtered them and threw the bodies into a pit.
But ten of the men begged Ishmael, “Do not kill us! We have hidden stores in the field: wheat, barley, olive oil, and honey.” So Ishmael spared them and left them out of the killing.

The pit Ishmael filled with the bodies of the men he killed along with Gedaliah{d} was a big one. King Asa had dug it to protect the land from Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael, Nethaniah’s son, crammed it with corpses.

Then Ishmael carried off the rest of the people of Mizpah as prisoners. They included the royal princesses and everyone else Nebuzaradan the guard commander had left in Gedaliah’s care. Ishmael son of Nethaniah led them away and set out to cross into Ammon.
Johanan son of Kareah heard about all Ishmael’s crimes, and so did the army officers who were with him.
They took all their men and marched out to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah. At the great pool in Gibeon, they found him.
The prisoners with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and the officers with him, and they cheered.
Every prisoner Ishmael had marched away from Mizpah turned around and went over to Johanan son of Kareah.
But Ishmael son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan, taking just eight men. He fled to Ammon.

Then Johanan son of Kareah and his army officers gathered all the survivors from Mizpah, the people he had saved from Ishmael son of Nethaniah after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah son of Ahikam. They were soldiers, women, children, and palace officials, brought back from Gibeon.
They moved on and camped at Geruth Chimham,{e} near Bethlehem. Their plan was to continue to Egypt,
away from the Chaldeans. They were afraid of those soldiers, because Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor of the land, had been murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah.

notes.text: Hebrew “the seventh month,” Tishri. The year is not given (maybe 587 or 586 B.C., or later).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “Salem.”
The signs of grief suggest people mourning for the ruined temple who still brought offerings to its site.
Hebrew “by the hand of Gedaliah,” perhaps “beside Gedaliah.” The Septuagint reads “the large pit.”
Or “the lodging place of Chimham” (compare 2 Samuel 19:37-40). The Septuagint reads “Gaberoch Chamaam.”

verses.text: All the army officers came up, among them Johanan son of Kareah and Jezaniah,{a} whose father was Hoshaiah. All the people came too, from the youngest to the oldest.
They said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Please hear our request. Pray to Yahweh your God for all of us who remain. We used to be many, but you can see that only a few of us are left.
Ask Yahweh your God to tell us which road to take and what to do.”
Jeremiah the prophet answered, “I hear you. I will pray to Yahweh your God just as you ask. Then I will tell you everything Yahweh replies. I will hold nothing back.”
They said to Jeremiah, “May Yahweh be a true and trusted witness against us if we do not do all that Yahweh your God sends you to tell us.
We will obey Yahweh our God, whether we like His answer or not. We are sending you to Him, and it will go well for us if we obey Yahweh our God.”
Ten days later, Yahweh gave Jeremiah a message.
Jeremiah called together Johanan son of Kareah, all the army officers with him, and everyone else, from the least important to the most important.
He told them, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says. You sent me to Him with your request, and here is His answer:
If you stay in this land, I will build you up and not tear you down. I will plant you firmly and not uproot you. I am sorry about the disaster I brought on you.{b}
Do not be afraid of Babylon’s king, though you fear him now. Do not be afraid of him,” Yahweh announces. “I am on your side, and I will free you from his power.
I will show you mercy, so that he will show you mercy and let you go back to your own land.
But you might say, ‘We will not stay in this land.’ You would then refuse to obey Yahweh your God.
You might insist, ‘No! We will go to Egypt. There we will see no war, hear no war trumpet, and never go hungry for bread. We will live there.’
If so, then hear what Yahweh says, you survivors of Judah. Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: If you are truly set on going to Egypt to live there,
then the sword you fear will overtake you in Egypt. The hunger you dread will follow close behind you there, and in Egypt you will die.
Everyone who is determined to go to Egypt to live will die by the sword, hunger, or sickness. None will survive or escape the disaster I will bring.

Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: I poured out My anger and fury on the people of Jerusalem. My fury will be poured out in the same way on you if you enter Egypt. You will become a curse, a horror, an insult, and a disgrace. You will never see this place again.
Yahweh has spoken to you, survivors of Judah: Do not go to Egypt. Be sure of this: I warned you today
that you have made a deadly mistake.{c} You yourselves were the ones who sent me to Yahweh your God. You said, ‘Pray for us to Yahweh our God. Whatever He says, tell us, and we will carry it out.’
I have told you today all that He said, but you disobeyed Yahweh your God in everything He sent me to tell you.
So know this for certain: you will die by the sword, by hunger, or by sickness, right where you wish to settle.”

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “Azariah son of Maaseiah” (compare 43:2, where the Hebrew also has Azariah).
Or “because I grieve over the disaster.” Hebrew nicham expresses a change of heart. It is often translated “repent.”
Or “you have fooled yourselves.” The Hebrew is uncertain.

subheads.1: The People Ask Jeremiah to Pray

verses.text: Jeremiah finished giving the people every message that Yahweh their God had sent him to deliver.

Azariah son of Hoshaiah and Johanan son of Kareah, together with all the proud men, answered Jeremiah. “You are lying! Yahweh our God never sent you to tell us, ‘Stay out of Egypt. Do not go there to live as foreigners.’
Baruch son of Neriah is the one turning you against us. He wants to put us in the Chaldeans’ hands, so they will kill us or drag us off to Babylon.”
So Johanan son of Kareah, together with every army officer and the whole crowd, refused to obey Yahweh’s command to remain in the land of Judah.

Instead, Johanan son of Kareah and all the army officers took away everyone who was left in Judah. These were the people who had come back to live in Judah from all the nations where they had been scattered.

They took the men, the women, the children, and the princesses. They took everyone Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, Shaphan’s grandson. They took the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch son of Neriah too.
They went into Egypt, because they would not obey Yahweh. They went as far as Tahpanhes.{a}
In Tahpanhes, Yahweh gave Jeremiah a message.
“Pick up some big stones. While the Judeans watch, bury them in the mortar{b} of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace in Tahpanhes.

Then tell them, ‘Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: I am sending for My servant Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon.{c} I will place his throne directly above these stones I have buried. He will spread his royal tent over them.
He will come and strike Egypt. Those meant for death will die. Those meant for exile will go away as prisoners. Those meant for the sword will be killed by it.

I{d} will light fires in the temples of Egypt’s gods. Nebuchadrezzar will burn the idols and carry off the gods. A shepherd picks lice out of his coat. In the same way, he will clean out Egypt and leave there in safety.
He will smash the sacred pillars{e} of Beth-Shemesh in Egypt. The temples of Egypt’s gods will go up in his flames.’”

notes.text: Tahpanhes was a fort city in the eastern Nile Delta. It is often thought to be Tell Defenneh (Greek Daphnae).
Hebrew malet, which is found only here. The meaning is uncertain (“mortar,” “clay,” or “pavement”).
The Septuagint does not have “My servant.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and other ancient versions read “He will set fire.”
Hebrew matstsevot, “standing stones” or “pillars.” Beth-Shemesh means “house of the sun.” It is Heliopolis, in northern Egypt.

verses.text: A message came to Jeremiah for all the Judeans who lived in Egypt: in Migdol, in Tahpanhes, in Memphis,{a} and across Pathros.{b}
“Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: You saw for yourselves all the disaster I brought on Jerusalem and every town of Judah. Today they are heaps of ruins, and nobody lives there.
This was because of the evil the people did to make Me angry. They went and burned incense to other gods and served them, gods that they, you, and your ancestors never knew.
I kept sending you My servants the prophets, day after day. They pleaded, ‘Please never do this disgusting thing that I hate!’
But nobody listened or cared. They kept on with their evil and kept offering incense to other gods.
So My anger and fury were poured out and blazed in Judah’s towns and in Jerusalem’s streets. They have turned into ruins and a wasteland, as they are today.
“Now Yahweh, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Why do you hurt yourselves so badly? You are removing men and women, children and babies from Judah. You will have nobody left.
Why do you anger Me with the idols you made? In Egypt, where you have settled, you burn incense to other gods. You will be destroyed. The whole world will use you as an example in curses and insults.
Have you forgotten the evil your ancestors did? Have you forgotten what the kings and queens{c} of Judah did, and what you and your wives did in Judah and on Jerusalem’s streets?
Even to this day they have not shown humility or respect. They have not lived by My teaching and rules, which I gave to you and your ancestors.
“So Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: I have turned against you to bring disaster, and I will wipe out all of Judah.

I will take the survivors of Judah who set their minds on moving to Egypt. In Egypt they will all come to an end. They will fall by the sword or die of hunger, from the least important to the most important. They will die by sword and hunger. They will become a curse, a horror, an insult, and a disgrace.
I will punish those who live in Egypt the way I punished Jerusalem, with sword, hunger, and sickness.
Not one of the Judean survivors who came to live in Egypt will escape or stay alive to go home. They long to return and settle in Judah, but they will not go back, except a few who run away.”{d}
All the men who knew their wives were burning incense to other gods stood up. So did all the women standing nearby, a huge crowd. All the people who lived in Pathros in Egypt replied to Jeremiah.
“We refuse to listen to the message you have given us in Yahweh’s name.

We will carry out everything we vowed. We will burn incense to the Queen of Heaven{e} and pour out drink offerings to her. Our ancestors did it, and so did our kings and our officials, in Judah’s towns and on Jerusalem’s streets. Back then we had plenty of bread, and we prospered. Disaster never came near us.
But since we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have had nothing. The sword and hunger have been wiping us out.”

The women added,{f} “When we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, our husbands knew about it. They knew we baked cakes stamped with her image{g} and poured out drinks to her.”
Then Jeremiah answered everyone who had spoken like that, the men and the women.

“Think about the incense you burned in Judah’s towns and Jerusalem’s streets. You did it, your ancestors did it, your kings and officials did it, and so did the common people. Do you think Yahweh forgot? Do you think He did not remember?
Yahweh could not put up with your evil deeds and disgusting acts any longer. So your land became a wasteland, a horror, and a curse. Nobody lives there, as you see today.
You burned incense and sinned against Yahweh. You did not obey Him or live by His teaching, rules, and warnings. That is why this disaster has come on you, as you see today.”
Jeremiah also said to all the people, including the women, “Hear Yahweh’s message, all you from Judah who are in Egypt.

Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: You and your wives said it with your mouths, and you did it with your hands. You said, ‘We will keep our vows to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her.’ Go ahead, then! Keep your vows and carry them out!

But hear Yahweh’s message, all you people of Judah in Egypt. Yahweh announces: I swear by My great name that no person from Judah anywhere in Egypt will ever again use My name in an oath, saying, ‘As the Lord Yahweh lives.’
I am watching over them to bring disaster, not good. The men of Judah in Egypt will die by sword and hunger until they are all gone.
Only a few will escape the sword and come back from Egypt to Judah. Then all the survivors of Judah who went to live in Egypt will learn whose word stands, Mine or theirs.
Here is the sign that I will punish you in this place,” Yahweh announces. “It will show you that My words against you will surely stand and bring disaster.

Yahweh says: I will give Pharaoh Hophra{h} king of Egypt to his enemies, who are trying to kill him. I gave Zedekiah king of Judah to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon in the same way. Nebuchadrezzar was Zedekiah’s enemy, and he wanted his life.”

notes.text: Hebrew Noph, Memphis, the old capital of Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo.
Pathros means Upper (southern) Egypt.
Hebrew “his wives.” The Septuagint reads “of your princes.”
Verses 1-14 are a sermon much like 7:1-15 and 11:1-17.
Probably the goddess Ishtar or Astarte (compare 7:18).
The Hebrew does not have this clause. It is added because the speakers are the women (“our husbands”).
Or “to shape her,” perhaps cakes made in the shape of the goddess or stamped with her picture.
Hophra is the Egyptian Wahibre (Greek Apries). He was pharaoh from 589 to 570 B.C. A revolt overthrew him.

subheads.7: Judah in Egypt Will Be Punished

verses.text: Jeremiah the prophet gave Baruch son of Neriah this message. It was the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, when Baruch wrote these words in a scroll while Jeremiah spoke them.{a}
“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this to you, Baruch:
You said, ‘How terrible for me! Yahweh has piled sorrow on top of my pain. I am tired out from groaning, and I find no rest.’
Tell him this: ‘Yahweh says: What I constructed, I am now demolishing. What I planted, I am now uprooting. This is true of the whole land.{b}

Are you chasing after great things for yourself? Stop chasing them. I am about to bring disaster on every living person,” Yahweh announces. “But wherever you go, I will let you keep your life as a prize.’”

notes.text: That is, 605-604 B.C., the year of chapter 36. This short message to Baruch is put here out of time order.
The Septuagint does not have “in the whole land.”

verses.text: Yahweh gave Jeremiah the prophet these words about the nations.{a}

About Egypt. Pharaoh Neco’s{b} army, from Egypt, had made camp at Carchemish,{c} beside the Euphrates River. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon crushed that army.

“Get your small shields and big shields ready.
March out to the fight!

Hitch up the horses.
Get on them, you riders!
Stand in line with your helmets on.
Sharpen your spears.
Put on your armor!

What is this I see?
They are terrified. They are backing away.
Their soldiers are beaten.
They run away in a rush,
and never look back.
Terror is all around!{d}” Yahweh announces.

“The fast cannot outrun it.
The strong cannot get away.
In the north, beside the Euphrates River,
they have tripped and fallen.

“Who is this, rising like the Nile,
like rivers with churning water?

Egypt rises like the Nile,
like rivers with churning water.
He said, ‘I will rise up and flood the land.
I will wipe out cities and their people.’

Charge ahead, horses!
Race wildly, chariots!
Send the warriors out:
men of Cush and Put who carry shields,
the men of Lud who pull back bows.{e}

That day belongs to the Lord Yahweh of Armies.
It is a day of payback, when He gets even with His enemies.
The sword will devour until it is full.
It will drink their blood until it has had enough.
The Lord Yahweh of Armies will hold a great killing
in the northern land beside the Euphrates River.

Go up to Gilead and find healing balm,
young woman of Egypt!
You have used many medicines for nothing.
You will not heal.

Nations have heard of your shame.
Your screams fill the earth.
One soldier trips over another,
and both fall down together.”
Yahweh gave Jeremiah the prophet a message about Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, who was coming to attack the land of Egypt.

“Announce it in Egypt. Spread it in Migdol.
Spread it in Memphis and Tahpanhes.
Say, ‘Take your places and be ready,
because the sword is eating up everything around you.’

Why have your strong ones been knocked down?{f}
They could not stand, because Yahweh pushed them over.

He made many stumble.
They collapsed on top of each other.
They said, ‘Get up! Let’s go home to our own people,
to the country of our birth,
and escape the cruel sword.’

There they cried, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is just a lot of noise.
He let the right time slip by.’{g}

As surely as I live,” announces the King,
whose name is Yahweh of Armies,
“one is coming as tall as Mount Tabor among the mountains,
as tall as Mount Carmel beside the sea.

Pack up your things to be taken away,
you who live in Egypt!
Memphis will become a wasteland,
a ruin with nobody living in it.

“Egypt is a beautiful young cow,
but a biting fly from the north has landed on her. It has landed!

The hired soldiers living in her
are like fattened calves.
They turn and run away together.
They do not hold their ground,
because their day of disaster has come.
The time for their punishment is here.

Egypt’s sound is like a snake sliding away,{h}
because the enemy marches with power.
They come against her with axes,
like men cutting wood.

They will chop down her forest,” Yahweh announces,
“even though nobody can get through it.
They are more than locusts.
They cannot be counted.

Egypt’s daughter is shamed.
She is handed over to a people from the north.”
Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Look, Amon of Thebes,{i} Pharaoh, and Egypt with her gods and kings will be punished by Me. Pharaoh and everyone who depends on him will be punished too.
I will give them to men who are hunting them, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. But later, people will live in Egypt again as in the old days,” Yahweh announces.{j}

“As for you, Jacob, My servant, do not be afraid.
Israel, do not lose heart.
Look, I will save you from a faraway place.
Your children will come home from the land where they are captives.
Jacob will return and rest in peace.
Nobody will frighten him.

Do not be afraid, Jacob, My servant,” Yahweh announces,
“because I am with you.
The nations where I scattered you
I will bring to a full end.
But I will not bring you to a full end.
I will correct you in a fair way,
but I will not leave you completely unpunished.”{k}

notes.text: Verse 1 is the title for the messages about the nations (chapters 46-51). The Septuagint does not have it.
Neco II ruled Egypt from 610 to 595 B.C. (compare 2 Kings 23:29-35).
Carchemish was on the upper Euphrates. Nebuchadnezzar beat the Egyptian army there in 605 B.C.
Hebrew magor missaviv. Compare 6:25; 20:3, 10.
Cush is the upper Nile region. Put is probably Libya. The Ludim may be Lydians or an African people.
The Hebrew word division is uncertain. The Septuagint divides the letters another way and reads “Why did Apis run away?”
Hebrew sha’on he’evir hamo’ed, a pun on Pharaoh’s name or title. The Septuagint just writes the Hebrew sounds in Greek letters.
Hebrew “her voice goes like the snake,” perhaps the hiss of a snake fleeing from woodcutters.
Amon was the chief god of No (Thebes) in Upper Egypt. The Septuagint reads “Ammon her son.”
The Septuagint does not have verse 26.
Verses 27-28 nearly repeat 30:10-11. Here the Septuagint has them.

verses.text: Yahweh gave Jeremiah the prophet this message about the Philistines, before Pharaoh attacked Gaza.{a}

Yahweh says:
“Watch! Water is rising in the north.
It is turning into a raging river.
It will cover the land and all that is in it,
the town and all who live there.
Everyone will scream,
and all who live in the land will howl

when they hear the pounding of his stallions’ hooves,
the rattling of his chariots, and the rumble of their wheels.
Fathers will not even turn to help their children.
Their hands are too weak.

It is because of the day that is coming
to wipe out every Philistine,
and to cut off from Tyre and Sidon
every helper still left.
Yahweh is wiping out the Philistines,
the survivors from the coast of Caphtor.{b}

Gaza has shaved her head in grief.
Ashkelon has been silenced.
Survivors of their lowland,{c}
how long will you cut yourselves?

‘Sword of Yahweh,’ they cry,
‘how long until you rest?
Go back into your case.
Be still and quiet!’

But how can it rest{d}
when Yahweh has given it orders?
He has sent it against Ashkelon
and the seacoast.”

notes.text: The time is not certain. It may be about Neco’s campaign around 609 B.C. The Septuagint does not have “that came.”
Caphtor is probably Crete or the area of the Aegean Sea, where the Philistines were said to come from (Amos 9:7).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “the rest of the Anakim.”
So the Septuagint and other ancient versions. The Hebrew reads “How can you rest.”

verses.text:
About Moab.{a}
Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says:
“Nebo is in trouble, because it is wrecked!
Kiriathaim is shamed and captured.
The fortress{b} is shamed and smashed.

Nobody praises Moab now.
In Heshbon men made evil plans against her:
‘Let’s wipe her out as a nation!’
You also, Madmen, will be silenced.
The sword will chase you.

Listen! A scream from Horonaim:
‘Ruin! Total destruction!’

Moab is broken.
Her little ones are crying out.

Up the hill of Luhith
people climb, sobbing the whole way.
Down the road from Horonaim
they hear screams of disaster.

Run! Save your lives!
Be like a desert shrub, left alone.{c}

You trusted in what you built and what you owned,
so you will be captured too.
Chemosh{d} will walk off into exile,
together with his priests and officials.

A destroyer will march into every town, and nobody will get away.
The valley will be ruined, and the high plain wrecked,
exactly as Yahweh said.

Give Moab wings,{e}
because she must fly away.
Her towns will become wastelands
with nobody living in them.

A curse on anyone who does Yahweh’s work lazily.
A curse on anyone who keeps his sword from shedding blood.

“Moab has lived in comfort since he was young.
He has sat undisturbed, like wine on its dregs.
Never was he emptied from one jar into another.
Never did he go into exile.
So his taste has stayed the same,
and his smell has not changed.

So look, days are coming,” Yahweh announces,
“when I will send men to pour him out.
They will empty his jars
and smash his pots.{f}

Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh,
just as Israel’s family was ashamed of Bethel, the god they trusted.{g}

“How can you say, ‘We are warriors,
brave men for the battle’?

The destroyer of Moab and her towns is on his way up.
Her finest young men are going down to the killing,”
says the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

Moab’s disaster is near.
Her ruin is racing toward her.

Mourn for her, all her neighbors,
all of you who know her fame.
Cry, ‘The strong rod is snapped!
The beautiful staff is broken!’

Step down from your glory
and sit in the thirsty dust,
you who live in Dibon!
The destroyer of Moab has come up against you.
He has wrecked your forts.

Stand beside the road and look,
you people of Aroer!
Ask the man who is running and the woman who is escaping,
‘What happened?’

Moab is shamed, because it is broken.
Wail and cry out!
Tell it along the Arnon River
that Moab has been wrecked.
“Judgment has come on the high plain. It has come on Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath.
It has come on Dibon and Nebo, and on Beth-Diblathaim.
It has also come on Kiriathaim, Beth-Gamul, and Beth-Meon,
and on Kerioth and Bozrah. It has come on every town in Moab, near or far.

Moab’s horn has been chopped off.
His arm has been broken,” Yahweh announces.

“Make him drunk,
because he made himself bigger than Yahweh.
Let Moab roll in his own vomit,
and let people laugh at him too.

Did you not laugh at Israel?
Was he caught among thieves,
that you shook your head
every time you spoke of him?

Leave your towns and live among the cliffs,
you people of Moab!
Be like a dove that builds her nest
on the sides of a canyon’s mouth.

We have heard about Moab’s pride.
He is extremely proud.
We have heard of his arrogance and his boasting,
and the stuck-up attitude of his heart.

I know how rude he is,” Yahweh announces.
“His bragging is false.
What he does is false.

I weep for you even more than for Jazer,
vine of Sibmah!
Your branches stretched over the sea.
They spread out as far as the sea of Jazer.{i}
A destroyer has pounced
on your summer fruit and your grape harvest.

Joy and gladness are gone
from the orchards and from Moab’s land.
I have stopped the wine flowing from the presses.
Nobody stomps the grapes with a happy shout.
The shouting is not a harvest cheer.

Heshbon cries out, and her voice reaches Elealeh and Jahaz.
It reaches from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-Shelishiyah,
because even Nimrim’s waters
have become a wasteland.

I will put an end in Moab,” Yahweh announces,
“to anyone who offers sacrifices at the high places
and burns incense to his god.

So my heart sounds like a mournful flute for Moab.
It sounds like a flute for the men of Kir-Heres.
The wealth they gathered is gone.

Every head is shaved.
Every beard is clipped.
Every hand is gashed.
Every waist is wrapped in rough cloth.

On every rooftop in Moab and in every town square
there is nothing but mourning.
I have smashed Moab
like a jar nobody wants,” Yahweh announces.

“How it is broken! How they howl!
See how Moab turns away in shame!
Moab has become a joke,
and a fright to all his neighbors.”

Kerioth{k} will be captured.
The forts will be taken.
On that day the courage of Moab’s warriors
will melt like that of a woman in labor.

Moab will be wiped out as a people,
because he made himself bigger than Yahweh.

Terror, pit, and trap{l}
wait for you, people of Moab,” Yahweh announces.

“Whoever runs from the terror
falls into the pit.
Whoever climbs out of the pit
is caught in the trap.
This is what I will bring on Moab,
the year they are punished,” Yahweh announces.

“In the shadow of Heshbon
the refugees stand helpless.{m}
A fire has burst out of Heshbon,
a flame from the city of Sihon.
It has burned up Moab’s forehead,
the skulls of the noisy sons of war.

Disaster for you, Moab!
The people of Chemosh are finished.
Your sons have been taken prisoner.
Your daughters have been taken into captivity.

But I will restore Moab’s fortunes
in the last days,” Yahweh announces.
That is the end of the judgment on Moab.

notes.text: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Much of this message is like Isaiah 15-16, and verses 45-46 are like Numbers 21:28-29 and 24:17.
Or “Misgab,” a place name.
Hebrew “like a juniper,” a desert shrub. Or “like Aroer.” The Septuagint has “like a wild donkey in the desert.”
Chemosh was the national god of Moab.
Hebrew tsits, usually “flower” or “wing.” The meaning is uncertain. Perhaps “salt” or “tombstone.”
The picture is of wine that has settled in the jar. Men now tip the jars and pour it out.
Bethel may be the town of the northern shrine, or the name of a god known from other ancient sources.
Kir-Heres means “wall of broken pottery.” It is probably the Moabite capital Kir-Hareseth (Isaiah 16:7, 11).
Some Hebrew copies and Isaiah 16:8 do not have “sea of.” The text is uncertain.
The Septuagint does not have the eagle picture here or the second half of verse 41.
Or “The towns.” Kerioth may be a place name or the plural “towns.”
Hebrew pachad wapachat wapach, a sound play. Compare Isaiah 24:17-18.
Verses 45-47 are not in the Septuagint.

verses.text:
About the Ammonites.{a}
Yahweh says:
“Has Israel no children?
Has he no one to take over his land?
Then why does Milcom{b} now own Gad,
with his people living in Gad’s towns?

So look, a time is coming,” Yahweh announces,
“when I will sound a battle cry
against Rabbah, the Ammonite capital.
It will become a heap of ruins.
The villages around it will go up in flames.
Then Israel will take back the land
from the people who took it from him,”
says Yahweh.

“Howl, Heshbon, because Ai is destroyed!
Scream, you daughters of Rabbah!
Put on rough cloth and mourn.
Run back and forth inside the walls of your sheep pens!
Milcom is going off into captivity,
with his priests and officials beside him.

Why are you proud of your valleys,
your valley that flows with plenty?{c} Unfaithful daughter,
you counted on your riches. You said,
‘Who would ever attack me?’

Look, I will bring terror on you
from everyone around you,”
announces the Lord Yahweh of Armies.
“Each of you will be chased away, going straight ahead,
and nobody will collect the runaways.

But later I will bring the Ammonites home from captivity,”
Yahweh announces.{d}

About Edom.{e}
Yahweh of Armies says:
“Is there no more wisdom in Teman?
Have the clever lost their good advice?
Has their wisdom spoiled?

Run! Turn around! Hide deep away,
you who live in Dedan!
I will bring disaster on Esau’s people
at the time I punish them.

If men came to pick your grapes,
would they not save a few for you?
If robbers came at night,
they would steal only what they wanted.{f}

But I have stripped Esau bare.
I have found his secret places,
so he cannot hide.
His children, relatives, and neighbors are wiped out,
and he is gone.

Leave your orphans. I will keep them alive.
Your widows can depend on Me.”
Yahweh says: “Look, people who did not deserve to drink the cup will drink it. Will you go unpunished? You will not go unpunished. You will surely drink it.
I swear by Myself,” Yahweh announces, “that Bozrah{g} will become a horror, an insult, a ruin, and a curse. All her towns will be ruins forever.”

A report from Yahweh has reached me.
An envoy has gone out among the nations:
“Gather your armies and march on her!
Get ready for battle!”

“Look, I will shrink you down among the nations.
People will look down on you.

The terror you cause has tricked you,
and so has your proud heart,
you who live in the cracks of the rocks,{h}
and hold the heights of the hill.
Even if you make your nest high like an eagle’s,
I will pull you down from there,”
Yahweh announces.

“Edom will become a horror.
Everyone who passes by will be shocked
and will whistle at all her wounds.

It will be like when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring towns were overturned,” says Yahweh.
“Nobody will live there.
Not one person will even camp there.

Look, like a lion coming up from the thick growth by the Jordan
to a pasture that is always green,
in an instant I will chase Edom off it.
I will put the one I choose in charge of it.
Who is like Me? Who can summon Me to court?
What shepherd can face Me?”

So hear the plan Yahweh has made against Edom,
and what He intends for the people of Teman.
The smallest of the flock will surely be dragged away.
Their pasture will be appalled by their fate.

At the sound of their fall, the earth shakes.
Their cry is heard at the Red Sea.{i}

“Look, like an eagle rising and diving,
someone will spread his wings over Bozrah.
On that day the strongest soldiers of Edom
will have hearts pounding like a woman’s in childbirth.”

About Damascus.
“Hamath and Arpad hang their heads in shame,
because they have heard bad news.
They melt with fear. The sea is troubled,{j}
and it cannot be calmed.

Damascus has become weak. She turns to run away.
Panic has grabbed her.
Pain and cramps have seized her,
like a woman in labor.

Why has the famous city not been abandoned,{k}
the town that made Me glad?

So her young men will fall in her town squares.
Every one of her soldiers will go quiet on that day,”
announces Yahweh of Armies.

“I will start a fire on the wall of Damascus.
Flames will eat the palaces of Ben-Hadad.”{l}

This is about Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor,{m} which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon attacked.
Yahweh says:
“Get up! March against Kedar!
Wipe out the eastern tribes!

They will seize the tents and flocks,
along with the curtains and every belonging.
They will drive off the camels as their own,
shouting at them, ‘Terror all around!’

Run! Go far away! Hide in deep places,
you people of Hazor,” Yahweh announces.
“Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, has a plan against you.
He has worked out a scheme against you.

Get up! March against a nation that is relaxing and living at ease,”
Yahweh announces.
“They have no gates or bars.
They live far from everyone.

Their camels will be taken.
Their large herds will be loot.
I will scatter to every wind those who cut their hair at the temples.{n}
Disaster will come on them from every direction,” Yahweh announces.

“Hazor will become a den for jackals,
a wasteland forever.
Nobody will live there.
No human being will stay there.”
Yahweh gave Jeremiah the prophet a message about Elam,{o} early in the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah.

Yahweh of Armies says:
“Look, I am breaking the bow of Elam,
the main source of their strength.

I will bring four winds against Elam
from the four corners of the sky.
I will scatter them in every direction.
There will be no nation
where Elam’s refugees do not go.

I will shatter Elam before her enemies,
before those who want to kill her.
I will pour out disaster on them,
My burning anger,” Yahweh announces.
“The sword will follow them
until I have wiped them out.

I will place My throne in Elam.
I will remove the king and the officials from there,”
Yahweh announces.

“But in the last days
I will restore Elam’s fortunes,”
Yahweh announces.

notes.text: Ammon was northeast of Moab. Its capital was Rabbah (today’s Amman). In the Septuagint the message about Ammon comes after the one about Kedar.
Milcom was the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5). The Hebrew vowels read malkam, “their king.”
Or “your fading valley.” The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “the plains of the Anakim.”
The Septuagint does not have verse 6.
Edom, south of the Dead Sea, came from Esau. Verses 9-10 and 14-16 are very much like Obadiah 1-5.
Or “would they not destroy only what was enough for them?”
Bozrah was a chief city of Edom.
Hebrew sela, “rock.” It may also be a play on the city Sela (2 Kings 14:7).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Or “there is worry like the sea.”
Or “How the city of praise has been abandoned!” Some versions do not have “not.”
Ben-Hadad means “son of Hadad.” Several Aramean kings of Damascus had this name.
Kedar was an Arabian tribe. Hazor here is probably a region of village settlements (Hebrew chatser), not the Hazor of Israel.
Or “who shave their temples.” Compare 9:26; 25:23.
Elam was east of Babylonia. In the Septuagint this message comes first among the messages about the nations.

subheads.28: A Message About Kedar and Hazor

verses.text: Through Jeremiah the prophet, Yahweh spoke this message about Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans.{a}

“Tell the nations. Spread the news.
Lift up a flag and announce it. Hide nothing.
Say, ‘Babylon has been captured.
Bel{b} is disgraced.
Merodach is smashed.
Her images are disgraced.
Her idols{c} are smashed.’

A nation is coming against her from the north.
It will turn her land into a wasteland
where nobody lives.
People and animals have run away and are gone.

“In those days and at that time,” Yahweh announces,
“Israel’s people will come,
and Judah’s people will come along with them.
They will cry as they walk,
and they will look for Yahweh their God.

They will ask for the road to Zion.
They will face that way and say,
‘Come, let’s bind ourselves to Yahweh
in an agreement that lasts forever and is never forgotten.’

My people have been lost sheep.
Their shepherds sent them wandering,
leaving them loose on the mountains.
They roamed from mountain to hill.
They forgot where they could rest.

Everyone who found them ate them up.
Their enemies said, ‘We have done nothing wrong,
because they sinned against Yahweh, their true pasture,
Yahweh, the hope of their ancestors.’

“Get out of Babylon!
Leave the Chaldeans’ country!
Be like the male goats that walk in front of the flock.

Look, I am stirring up an alliance of great nations
from the northern land, and sending them against Babylon.
They will line up to face her.
She will be captured from that direction.
Their arrows are like those of an expert{d} soldier
who never comes home empty-handed.

The land of Chaldea will be robbed.
All who rob her will have their fill,” Yahweh announces.

“You rejoice and celebrate,
you who looted what belongs to Me.
You jump like a calf in the grain,
and neigh like stallions.

But your mother will be terribly ashamed.
The one who gave you birth will be disgraced.
Look, she will rank last among the nations,
a dry, empty desert.

Yahweh’s anger will leave her empty of people.
She will be completely deserted.
Everyone who walks by Babylon will be shocked
and will hiss at all her wounds.

Take your positions around Babylon,
all you who pull back the bow.
Shoot at her! Save no arrows,
because she has sinned against Yahweh.

Shout at her from all sides:
‘She gives up!{e}
Her towers have fallen.
Her walls are torn down.’
This is Yahweh’s payback.
Pay her back!
Do to her what she did to others.

Cut off from Babylon the person who plants seed,
and the person who swings the sickle at harvest.
Because of the cruel sword,{f}
each one will turn back to his own people,
and each will flee to his own land.

“Israel is a scattered flock,
chased off by lions.
First the king of Assyria ate him up.
Last of all, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon has crunched his bones.

So Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says:
Look, I will punish Babylon’s king and his land,
in the same way that I punished Assyria’s king.

Israel I will lead back to his own pasture.
He will graze on Carmel and Bashan.
He will eat until he is full
on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.

In those days and at that time,” Yahweh announces,
“people will search for Israel’s guilt, and find none.
They will search for Judah’s sins, and find none,
because I will forgive the survivors I leave alive.

“Attack the land of Merathaim.{g}
Attack it and the people of Pekod.
Kill them and destroy them completely,” Yahweh announces.
“Do everything I have ordered you.

The noise of war is in the land.
Great destruction is here!

How the hammer that beat the whole world
is chopped down and broken!
What a horror Babylon has become
among the nations!

You were caught in a trap I laid, Babylon,
and you never knew it.
You were found and seized,
because you fought against Yahweh.

Yahweh has opened His storeroom.
He has taken out the weapons of His anger,
because the Lord Yahweh of Armies has work to carry out
in the land of the Chaldeans.

Attack her from the farthest edge.
Break open her barns.
Pile her up like grain bundles and set her apart for destruction.
Leave nothing of her.

Kill all her bulls.
Let them go down to the slaughter.
They are doomed! Their day has come,
the time they will be punished.

“Listen! Refugees are escaping from the land of Babylon.
They come to Zion to announce
that Yahweh our God is paying back,
paying back for His temple.{h}

Call archers to Babylon,
all who pull back the bow.
Make camp on every side of her.
Let nobody get away.
Pay her back for what she did.
Treat her the way she treated others,
because she was proud against Yahweh,
against Israel’s Holy One.

So her young men will fall in her town squares.
Every soldier of hers will be silenced on that day,” Yahweh announces.

“Look, I am against you, Pride,{i}”
announces the Lord Yahweh of Armies.
“Your day has come,
the time when I punish you.

Proud one, you will stumble and fall,
and nobody will pick you up.
I will light a fire in your towns,
and it will burn up everything around you.”

Yahweh of Armies says this:
“Israel’s people are oppressed,
and so are Judah’s people.
All who captured them hold on tightly.
They refuse to let them go.

But their Rescuer is strong.
His name is Yahweh of Armies.
He will certainly fight their case.
He will give rest to the earth
and trouble to the people of Babylon.

A sword against the Chaldeans,” Yahweh announces,
“against the people who live in Babylon,
against her leaders and her thinkers!

A sword against her fortune-tellers,{j} and they will become fools!
A sword against her heroes, and they will break with fear!

A sword against her horses and chariots,
and against all the foreign soldiers in her,
so they become like women!
A sword against her treasures, and robbers will take them!

Heat{k} will come upon her waters, and they will dry up!
Hers is a land of carved idols,
and they go wild over frightening statues.

So desert animals and jackals will live there,
and ostriches will live in her.
Nobody will ever live in her again
or settle there, from one age to the next.{l}

It will be like when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns near them,” Yahweh announces.
“Nobody will live there.
No person will stay in her.

Bows and spears are their weapons.
They are cruel and show no pity.
Their noise is like the roaring sea.
They ride on horses,
lined up like one man for battle
against you, Babylon!

The king of Babylon has been told about them.
His hands have gone limp.
Pain has gripped him,
like the pain of a woman in labor.

“Look, like a lion coming up from the thick growth by the Jordan
to a pasture that is always green,{n}
in an instant I will chase them off it.
I will put the one I choose in charge of it.
Who is like Me? Who can summon Me to court?
What shepherd can face Me?

Listen to the plan Yahweh has made against Babylon,
and the purposes He has formed against the land of the Chaldeans:
the smallest of the flock will surely be dragged away.
Their pasture will be appalled by their fate.

At the news that Babylon is captured, the earth shakes,
and a cry is heard among the nations.”

notes.text: The Septuagint begins simply “The word of Yahweh that He spoke against Babylon.”
Bel (“lord”) and Merodach (Babylonian Marduk) are names of the chief god of Babylon.
Hebrew gillulim, an insulting word, perhaps “dung pellets.”
So many Hebrew copies and ancient versions. Other Hebrew copies read “a childless-making.”
That is, she surrenders.
Or “the dove’s sword.” The Septuagint reads “the Greek sword.”
Merathaim means “double rebellion” and Pekod means “punishment.” They are word plays on Babylonian place names.
The Septuagint does not have “revenge for His temple.”
Hebrew zadon, a word for pride, spoken to as if it were a person.
Hebrew baddim, “empty talkers,” that is, men who gave messages for the gods.
Hebrew choreb, a sound play on cherev, “sword,” in verses 35-37. Some read “sword” here too.
Compare Isaiah 13:20-22; 34:13-15.
Verses 41-43 reuse 6:22-24, once said about Zion and now said about Babylon.
Verses 44-46 reuse 49:19-21, once said about Edom.

verses.text:
Yahweh says:
“Watch! I am raising up a destroying wind
against Babylon
and against Leb-Kamai’s people.{a}

I will send strangers to Babylon who will blow her away like chaff.
They will empty out her land.
They will surround her on every side
on her day of disaster.

Let the archer string his bow{b}
against the soldier who struts in his armor.
Show her young men no pity.
Set her whole army apart for destruction.

They will drop dead across the land of the Chaldeans,
run through with swords in her streets.

Israel and Judah have not been abandoned
as widows by their God, Yahweh of Armies,
though their land is full of guilt
against Israel’s Holy One.

Run out of Babylon!
Each person must save his own life!
Do not die for her guilt,
because it is time for Yahweh’s revenge.
He is paying her what she has earned.

Babylon was a golden cup in Yahweh’s hand,
and she made the whole earth drunk.
Nations drank from her wine,
so nations went insane.

Babylon has suddenly fallen and been shattered.
Cry out over her!
Bring medicine for her pain.
She might still recover.

We tried to heal Babylon,
but she would not be healed.
Leave her. Let each of us go
home to his own country,
because her judgment reaches up to the sky,
as high as the clouds.

Yahweh has proved us right.
Come, let’s announce in Zion
what Yahweh our God has done.

“Whet the arrows!
Fill the quivers!{c}
The minds of the kings of the Medes{d} have been roused by Yahweh,
for His plan against Babylon is to wipe it out.
This is Yahweh getting even,
getting even for His temple.

Lift a battle flag against the walls of Babylon.
Make the guard stronger.
Post the lookouts.
Set up the ambushes.
Yahweh planned this, and He has done
what He said about the people of Babylon.

You who live beside many rivers
and have so many treasures,
your end has come.
The line is drawn on your dishonest profits.{e}

Yahweh of Armies has sworn by His own name:
‘I will certainly fill you with soldiers, as if with locusts,
and they will shout in triumph over you.’

When He thunders, the waters in the sky roar.
Clouds rise at His command from the edges of the earth.
He makes lightning for the rain
and brings the wind out of His storerooms.

Everyone is foolish and has no knowledge.
Every goldsmith is shamed by his idol,
because his cast figure is a lie.
It has no breath in it.

They are worthless, something to laugh at.
When they are judged, they will disappear.

Jacob’s Portion is not like these things,
because He formed everything.
Israel is the tribe He calls His own.{g}
His name is Yahweh of Armies.

“You are My war club,{h} My weapon for battle.
With you I smash nations.
With you I wreck kingdoms.

With you I smash horses and riders.
With you I smash chariots and drivers.

With you I smash men and women.
With you I smash old people and boys.
With you I smash young men and girls.

With you I smash shepherds and flocks.
With you I smash plowmen and their oxen.
With you I smash governors and officials.

“Look, I am against you, destroying mountain,” Yahweh announces,
“you who destroy the whole earth.
My hand will reach out to you.
I will push you down the cliffs
and turn you into a charred mountain.

Nobody will take a stone from you for a corner,
or a stone for a base.
You will be a ruin forever,” Yahweh announces.

“Raise a flag in the land.
Blow the horn among the nations.
Prepare nations to fight her.
Call kingdoms against her:
Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz.{i}
A commander must be chosen to lead the attack.
Send horses up like swarms of bristling locusts.

Prepare nations to fight her,
the kings of the Medes,
their governors and all their officers,
and every country they rule.

The land shakes and twists in pain,
because Yahweh’s plans against Babylon stand firm.
They will make the land of Babylon a wasteland
where nobody lives.

Babylon’s warriors have stopped fighting.
They sit in their forts.
Their strength has drained away.
They have turned into women.
Her homes are burning.
Her gate bars are broken.

One runner meets another,
and one messenger meets another,
to tell the king of Babylon
that his city is taken from one end to the other.

The river crossings are seized.
The reed marshes{j} are burning.
The soldiers are terrified.”

Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says:
“Babylon, the city, is like a threshing floor
when the grain is being stamped flat.
Only a short time remains,
and then her harvest will come.”

“Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon has devoured me.{k}
He has thrown me into confusion.
He has left me like an empty jar.
Like a monster of the sea he gulped me down.
He filled up on my finest food,
and then he washed me away.

‘Let the violence done to me and my flesh come down on Babylon,’
the people of Zion will say.
‘Let my blood come down on the people of Chaldea,’
Jerusalem will say.”

So Yahweh says:
“Look, I will argue your case
and get revenge for you.
I will dry up her sea
and make her spring run dry.

Babylon will become a pile of ruins,
a den for jackals,
something people stare at and hiss at,
with nobody living there.{l}

They all roar like lions.
They growl like lion cubs.

While they are hot with excitement, I will serve them a feast
and make them drunk so they will celebrate.
Then they will sleep a sleep that never ends
and never wake,” Yahweh announces.

“I will drag them down like lambs to the butcher,
like rams and goats.

“How Sheshach{m} has been captured!
The glory of the whole earth is seized!
What a horror Babylon has become
among the nations!

The sea has risen against Babylon.
Its roaring waves cover her.

Her towns have become ruins,
a dry land, a flat desert,
a land where nobody lives
and no human passes through.

Bel in Babylon I will punish,
and make him spit up what he swallowed.
Nations will no longer stream to him like a river.
Babylon’s wall has fallen.

Do not lose heart.
Do not be afraid of the rumors in the land.
One rumor comes this year,
and another the next year,
with violence in the land,
and one ruler against another.

So watch, the days are coming
when I will punish Babylon’s carved gods.
Her whole country will be shamed,
and all her dead will lie inside her.

Then sky and earth and everything in them
will sing for joy over Babylon,
because destroyers will come against her from the north,”
Yahweh announces.

“Babylon must fall because of the people Israel lost in war,
just as the dead of all the earth fell because of Babylon.

You who escaped the sword,
go! Do not stand still!
Remember Yahweh in the far country.
Let Jerusalem be on your mind.

‘We feel shame, for we have heard taunts.
Disgrace covers our faces,
because foreigners have walked into
the holy places of Yahweh’s house.’

So look, days are coming,” Yahweh announces,
“when I will punish her idols.
All over her land the wounded will groan.

Even if Babylon climbed up to the sky,
and even if she made her high fortress strong,
I would send destroyers against her,”
Yahweh announces.

“Listen! A scream from Babylon!
Great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!

Yahweh is wrecking Babylon
and ending her loud noise.
Enemy waves roar like great waters.
The sound of their voices booms.

Yes, a destroyer has come against Babylon.
Her warriors are captured.
Their bows are snapped,
because Yahweh is a God who pays back.
He will collect in full.

Her officials and wise men I will make drunk,
her governors, her deputies, and her soldiers.
They will sleep a sleep that never ends and will not get up,”
announces the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

“Yahweh of Armies says:
The wide wall of Babylon
will be torn flat,
and her tall gates
will be burned.
So peoples work for nothing,
and nations tire themselves out only to feed the fire.”{o}

Jeremiah the prophet gave Seraiah{p} a message. Seraiah’s father was Neriah, and his grandfather was Mahseiah. Seraiah traveled to Babylon with Zedekiah king of Judah during the fourth year Zedekiah ruled. Seraiah was the officer in charge of arranging the camp.{q}
On a single scroll Jeremiah wrote every disaster that would fall on Babylon. These were all the words about Babylon.
Jeremiah told Seraiah, “Once you reach Babylon, make sure you read all these words aloud.
Then say, ‘Yahweh, You have declared that this place will be cut off, so that nothing living remains in it, neither person nor animal. It will be empty forever.’
When you have read the whole scroll, tie a rock to it and toss it into the Euphrates, in the deep middle.

Then say, ‘Babylon will go down like this and never come back up, because of the disaster I am about to bring. And they will be worn out.’”{r}
These are the words of Jeremiah, up to here.

notes.text: Leb-Kamai means “the heart of those who rise against me.” It is an atbash code for Kasdim, “Chaldeans.” Atbash swaps each Hebrew letter with its mirror letter in the alphabet.
The Hebrew letters repeat “bend.” The Hebrew vowels and some ancient versions read it a different way.
Or “Pick up the shields.”
The Medes came from northwestern Iran. They helped overthrow Assyria and later became part of the Persian empire.
Hebrew “the cubit (ammah) of your cutting off,” a way of saying the measure of a life or of gain. The meaning is uncertain.
Verses 15-19 repeat 10:12-16.
So many Hebrew copies and 10:16. The Hebrew here does not have “Israel is.”
Hebrew mappets, “smasher.” The speaker is talking to Babylon (or possibly Cyrus). The verb “smash” appears ten times in verses 20-23.
Ararat (Urartu, near Lake Van), Minni (the Mannaeans), and Ashkenaz (the Scythians) were peoples to the north of Babylon.
Hebrew agammim, “pools” or “reed thickets.”
So the Hebrew reading in the margin. The written text reads “us” throughout this verse. Zion is speaking here.
The Septuagint shortens verse 37: “Babylon will be a ruin and nobody will live in her.”
Sheshach is an atbash code for Babel (Babylon). See 25:26. The Septuagint does not have the name here.
Verses 45-48 are not in the Septuagint. Verse 49 there begins “and in Babylon the dead of the whole earth will fall.”
Compare Habakkuk 2:13. The Septuagint reverses the meaning: “and the peoples will not work for nothing.”
Seraiah means “Yahweh is prince.” He was the brother of Baruch (compare 32:12). The Septuagint reads “Saraias.”
Hebrew sar menuchah, “officer of the resting place,” that is, the one in charge of the king’s lodging on the trip.
The Septuagint does not have “and they will be worn out” or the last line about the words of Jeremiah.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one when he took the throne, and Jerusalem was his capital for eleven years.{a} Hamutal, a woman of Libnah and daughter of a man named Jeremiah, was his mother.
Zedekiah did evil in Yahweh’s sight, just as Jehoiakim had done.{b}
It was Yahweh’s anger that brought all this on Jerusalem and Judah. In the end He drove them away from His presence. Zedekiah had also rebelled against Babylon’s king.

In Zedekiah’s ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month (December–January),{c} Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came to attack Jerusalem. He brought his whole army, camped outside the city, and built ramps against it all the way around.
Zedekiah’s eleventh year arrived before the attack on the city let up.
In the fourth month (June–July),{d} on day nine, hunger inside the city got terrible. The people had no food left.

Then the walls were broken open. At night the soldiers all slipped out through the gate that stood between the two walls, next to the king’s garden. The Chaldeans were circling the city, but the soldiers headed for the Arabah.{e}
The Chaldean army chased the king and caught up with Zedekiah on the plains near Jericho. All his soldiers left him and scattered.
The Chaldeans arrested the king and marched him to Riblah, in the land of Hamath, where Babylon’s king was staying. He decided Zedekiah’s punishment there.
While Zedekiah watched, Babylon’s king killed Zedekiah’s sons. He killed all the leaders of Judah too, right there.
Then he put out Zedekiah’s eyes and chained him with bronze chains. Babylon’s king took him to Babylon and held him in a jail{f} till Zedekiah’s death.

It was the tenth day of the fifth month (July–August),{g} in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon, when Nebuzaradan came into Jerusalem. He was the chief of the royal guard and served the king of Babylon.
He burned down Yahweh’s house, the king’s palace, and every house in Jerusalem. Every important building went up in flames.
The entire Chaldean army that came with the chief of the guard pulled down all the walls around Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan, the chief of the guard, took some of the poorest people into exile. He also took everyone else still in the city, those who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the skilled workers.{h}
He did leave a few of the poorest country people to care for the vineyards and fields.
The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars that stood at Yahweh’s house. They also broke up the carts and the huge bronze tank called the Sea. They hauled all that bronze away to Babylon.
They took the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, and dishes, along with all the bronze tools used in the temple service.

The chief of the guard also took the small cups, the fire pans, the sprinkling bowls, the pots, the lamp stands, the dishes, and the bowls for pouring out drinks. Whatever was made of solid gold or of silver, he carried off.
There was too much bronze to weigh. It came from the two pillars, from the huge tank, from the twelve bronze bulls under that tank,{i} and from the carts King Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house.
Each pillar stood twenty-seven feet tall.{j} A cord eighteen feet long could wrap around it. It was hollow, and its walls were about three inches thick.

On top of one pillar sat a bronze top piece that was seven and a half feet tall.{k} Bronze net work and pomegranates covered it all around. The other pillar had the same design, with pomegranates too.
Ninety-six pomegranates hung on the sides.{l} In all, one hundred pomegranates were set on the net work around the top.
Nebuzaradan seized the chief priest Seraiah and the priest who ranked next, Zephaniah. He also seized the three men who guarded the doors.

Out of the city he also took the officer who had led the soldiers. Seven of the king’s personal advisers{m} were found in the city, and he took them. He took the secretary of the army commander, who signed up the people for service. And sixty ordinary men still in the city were taken as well.
Nebuzaradan, the chief of the guard, led them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
At Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them struck down and killed. In this way Judah was taken away from its own land.
Here are the numbers of people Nebuchadrezzar took into exile:{n} In his seventh year he took 3,023 people of Judah.
Eighteen years into his rule, 832 people from Jerusalem went.
In his twenty-third year Nebuzaradan, the chief of the guard, took 745 people of Judah into exile. The total came to 4,600 people.

Thirty-seven years after Jehoiachin king of Judah was taken away, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month (February–March),{o} Evil-Merodach{p} became king of Babylon. That same year he showed kindness to Jehoiachin and let him out of prison.
He spoke gently to Jehoiachin. He gave him a seat of honor higher than the seats of the other kings staying with him in Babylon.
Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes. All through his life he dined at the king’s own table.
The king of Babylon gave Jehoiachin a daily allowance for as long as he lived, right up to the day he died.{q}

notes.text: Zedekiah’s rule was about 597–586 B.C. Jeremiah 52 follows 2 Kings 24:18–25:30 closely, with a few differences.
Verses 2–3 are not in the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation.
The Hebrew names the month Tevet. This was January 588 B.C. The Septuagint says “the ninth month.”
The Hebrew names the month Tammuz. This was July 586 B.C. (some date it to 587). The Septuagint does not have “in the fourth month.”
The Arabah is the rift valley of the Jordan River.
The Hebrew says “house of punishment.” The Septuagint says “the grinding-house.”
The Hebrew names the month Av. This was August 586 B.C. 2 Kings 25:8 says “the seventh day.” The Septuagint does not have this date.
Verse 15 is not in the Septuagint.
2 Kings 25:16 does not mention “the twelve bronze bulls.”
The Hebrew says “eighteen cubits” (about 27 feet). The cord was “twelve cubits” (about 18 feet), and the thickness was “four fingers” (about 3 inches).
The Hebrew says “five cubits,” about 7.5 feet. 2 Kings 25:17 says “three cubits.”
The Hebrew may mean “facing the winds,” toward the four directions. The meaning is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “seven men who saw the king’s face.” 2 Kings 25:19 says five.
Verses 28–30 are not in the Septuagint or in 2 Kings 25. The dates probably count from 597, 586, and 581 B.C.
The Hebrew names the month Adar. This was March 561 B.C. 2 Kings 25:27 says “the twenty-seventh day.”
Evil-Merodach is the Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk.” He was Nebuchadrezzar’s son and ruled 562–560 B.C.
The book ends with Jehoiachin alive and honored in exile. This is a quiet sign of hope for David’s family line.
